title: Canny — turning gradients into clean edges
description: From a fuzzy Sobel magnitude to a one-pixel-wide binary edge map. The Canny pipeline: blur, gradient, non-max suppression, hysteresis thresholding.

data.markdown:
## Where Sobel falls short

In Lesson 1 we saw that the Sobel gradient magnitude lights up at edges — but it also lights up everywhere there is texture or noise, and every edge ends up several pixels thick. For real applications (object detection, vectorisation, shape descriptors) we usually want:

1. A **binary** edge map: each pixel is either "edge" or "not edge".
2. Edges that are **one pixel wide** (thin), not fuzzy ramps.
3. **Connected** edges where possible — a real boundary should not be broken into dotted fragments.

The **Canny edge detector** (John F. Canny, 1986) was designed to satisfy all three with a four-step pipeline. The good news: in OpenCV it is one function call, `cv2.Canny`.

## The four steps Canny performs internally

1. **Gaussian blur.** Smooth the image to suppress high-frequency noise so the gradient is computed on stable values. OpenCV applies this implicitly before the gradient.
2. **Sobel gradient.** Compute $G_x$, $G_y$, magnitude and **direction** $\theta = \arctan(G_y / G_x)$. We need direction this time — Sobel alone did not use it.
3. **Non-maximum suppression (NMS).** For each pixel, look at its two neighbours along the gradient direction. Keep the pixel only if its magnitude is larger than both neighbours. This thins fuzzy edges into one-pixel-wide ridges.
4. **Hysteresis thresholding.** Use two thresholds, `low` and `high`. Pixels above `high` are *strong* edges (definitely kept). Pixels below `low` are dropped. Pixels in between are *weak*: kept only if they are 8-connected to a strong edge. This bridges gaps without picking up isolated noise.

The `low:high` ratio is typically `1:2` or `1:3`. OpenCV's docs recommend `1:3`. The values are in the same units as the gradient magnitude — usually 50–200 for an 8-bit input.

data.taskMarkdown:
All four steps above are bundled into a single OpenCV call. The two numeric arguments are the lower and upper hysteresis thresholds (in the gradient-magnitude units).

```
edges = cv2.Canny(img, threshold1=100, threshold2=200)
```

Returns a `uint8` array the same shape as `img`: `255` where there is an edge, `0` otherwise. Try the snippet below, then compare with the output figure underneath — and try lowering the thresholds (e.g. `30, 60`) to see how many faint edges Canny picks up.

The Code widget mounts the reference scene shown on the left at `/inputs/input-canny.png`, so `cv2.imread` works just like on disk. This lesson runs **real OpenCV** in the lesson's Python kernel, so `cv2.Canny` produces exactly the pixel values you'd get from `opencv-python` on your own machine.
data.starterCode:
import cv2
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Load the input scene from /inputs/ — the Code widget mounted the
#    PNG shown on the left into Pyodide's virtual filesystem before
#    your code ran, so cv2.imread works exactly as it would on disk.
img = cv2.imread('/inputs/input-canny.png', cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)

# 2. Canny does Gaussian blur + Sobel + NMS + hysteresis internally.
#    Lower threshold ~ how weak an edge we'll keep if connected.
#    Upper threshold ~ how strong an edge needs to be to start a chain.
#    The 1:2 / 1:3 ratio is the rule of thumb from Canny's original paper.
edges = cv2.Canny(img, 100, 200)

plt.imshow(edges, cmap='gray')
plt.axis('off')

tests.name: canny_edges_are_binary
tests.body: assert set(int(v) for v in np.unique(edges).tolist()) <= {0, 255}

import cv2
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

img = cv2.imread('/inputs/input-canny.png', cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)

edges = cv2.Canny(img, 100, 200)

plt.imshow(edges, cmap='gray')
plt.axis('off')

inputs.alt: A synthetic grayscale scene with two houses on a graded sky background. The bottom of the frame is filled with a checkerboard pattern. The image has photographic blur and noise added.
inputs.caption: Figure 2.1 — Synthetic textured scene (256×256, grayscale). The two houses give us crisp object boundaries; the checkered floor lets us watch Canny suppress the high-frequency texture; the smooth sky gradient lets us check that Canny does NOT fire on slow ramps.

outputMedia.alt: Binary edge map: the outlines of the two houses, their roofs, windows, doors, and the horizon line all appear as crisp white one-pixel-wide curves. The checkerboard pattern at the bottom is reduced to the boundaries of each square. The smooth sky gradient produces no edges at all.
outputMedia.caption: Figure 2.2 — `cv2.Canny(img, 100, 200)` applied to Figure 2.1. Note three things: (1) the smooth sky gradient produces no edges — slow ramps are correctly ignored; (2) the texture in the checkerboard is reduced to the boundaries of each tile; (3) every kept edge is one pixel wide.

sections.title: Sobel vs Canny — when to use which

data.markdown:
## Sobel vs Canny

| | **Sobel** | **Canny** |
|---|---|---|
| Output | continuous magnitude `[0..255]` | binary `0` or `255` |
| Width | several px (gradient "ramp") | one px (after NMS) |
| Noise handling | none — passes through | implicit Gaussian blur + hysteresis |
| Speed | one convolution per direction | ~3× more work (blur + NMS + BFS) |
| Typical use | feature input to ML models; HOG-style descriptors | object outlining, contour extraction, vectorisation |

A rule of thumb: if your *downstream code* will threshold the result anyway, give it the Sobel magnitude and let it choose. If you need clean edges *now* — say, to feed `cv2.findContours` — use Canny.

### Tuning the thresholds

`cv2.Canny`'s two arguments are the only knobs you usually touch. Practical workflow:

1. Start with `(100, 200)`.
2. If you are missing real edges → lower **both** by ~30%.
3. If you are picking up texture/noise → raise **both** by ~30%.
4. Keep the `1:2` or `1:3` ratio between them; varying the ratio independently rarely helps.
